title: Continuous annealing of medium-Mn steels: design of sustainable manufacturing and “rapid investigation” of heat treatment
abstract: Abstract Manufacturing including intercritical processing of medium-Mn sheet steels is usually a multi-hour batch-type annealing with low environmental and economic indicators. It additionally influences severe variability of mechanical properties of steel depending on a distance from the center of the coil, and thus material waste. For this reason, car body elements with high quality requirements cannot be effectively manufactured in such a process. There is a research gap and an industry need for a sustainable time- and cost-effective production process that can be implemented on a large scale in industry, using existing installations. For this reason, the process of designing and optimizing the conditions of heat treatment of medium-Mn steel in a continuous-annealing mode was performed, which assumes soaking in less than 120 s. During the research, heating conditions were developed that can be achieved using a conventional electric furnace. To experimentally and time-effectively optimize the temperature–time conditions in terms of mechanical properties, a novel method of “rapid investigation” of heat treatment was proposed and implemented. This method using a dilatometer allows for high-precision, time-efficient and waste-reducing optimization of heat treatment of newly designed steels. The research showed the full possibility of introducing continuous annealing into the heat treatment of advanced medium-Mn steel. A slight change in thermal parameters allowed formation of lath like microstructures with different thickness and stability of RA and thus a wide control of both the strength (YS, UTS) and plasticity of steel (TEl) up to the UTS x TEl threshold of 37 GPa%. This suggests the possibility of applying the presented heat treatment conditions to the industrial production of steel for various applications.
journal: Archives of Civil and Mechanical Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The limitation of conventional steels is their decreasing plasticity with increasing strength [ 1 ,  2 ]. Since the early 1990s, the automotive industry has been in great demand for steels that combine high strength and good plasticity. A breakthrough step was incorporating metastable retained austenite (RA) into the steel microstructure [ 3 ,  4 ]. Thanks to its strain-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) [ 5 ], it was possible to obtain unprecedented strain hardening in steel products [ 6 ]. This allowed to effectively delay the formation of the neck and thus increase the plasticity, while maintaining high strength or even its simultaneous increase. It opened the way to production of materials with new levels of mechanical properties [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ], and thus reduce its required weight in modern cars [ 10 ]. A new approach to the design of the chemical composition and heat treatment resulted in the development of Advanced High Strength Steels (AHSS) [ 11 ] with the newest developments such as medium-Mn steels belonging to the 3rd generation of AHSS [ 12 ]. Medium-Mn steels, due to their optimized chemical composition and specialized heat treatment, allowed to eliminate most of the disadvantages of their predecessors–high-Mn steels [ 13 ]. The limitation of the Mn content to the range of 3% to 12% made it possible to reduce its usage decrease the production costs [ 14 ]. It also increases the corrosion resistance and reduces the tendency to chemical segregation of Mn. In addition, reducing the content of this element results in limiting the impact of plastic instability (PLC effect) during deformation. Medium-Mn steels appear to be almost free of casting and hot working problems, which occurred in steels with higher manganese contents. On the other hand, medium-Mn steels show strength and plasticity that may go beyond those of other multiphase steels from the 1st AHSS generation [ 12 ,  15 ]. This results in the recent introduction of pilot batches to steelworks [ 16 ], despite the relatively short time since their invention.

Medium-Mn steels are characterized by a fine grain size and a fraction of metastable RA reaching over 20%. The high fraction of this phase contributes significantly to their plastic properties, which may reach over 25% at a high-strength level of over 800 MPa [ 17 ]. During the plastic deformation process, the metastable austenite undergoes martensitic transformation or/and intense mechanical twinning. Both processes provide increased plasticity without the loss of steel’s strength [ 16 ]. Currently, one of the most promising strategies of heat treatment of medium-Mn steels is intercritical annealing [ 16 ,  18 ]. It is applied as a separate isothermal holding in the range between A c1  and A c3  temperatures, at which some fraction of austenite forms and is enriched by C and Mn from ferrite or tempered martensite. The properly designed and performed intercritical annealing should result in full stability of austenite at room temperature. Therefore, after final cooling the microstructure consists of ferrite (or highly tempered martensite) and RA [ 19 ]. In hot-rolled medium-Mn steels the dominating mechanism is so-called ART (austenite reverted transformation) process. The initial martensitic microstructure controls the nucleation and growth of austenite. After crossing the A c1  temperature, austenite starts to form on martensite lath boundaries, and triple joints, which act like nucleation sites. The C and Mn atoms tend to segregate to these areas [ 16 ]. The newly formed austenite grains start to grow along laths of tempered martensite. The austenite inherits therefore the morphology of parent martensite, so the final morphology of both phases after the process completion is lamellar [ 20 ]. It is favorable as it allows to eliminate the discontinuous yielding behavior, which is a disadvantage of cold-rolled equiaxed-grain medium-Mn steels [ 21 ].

Most of the studies on intercritically annealed medium-Mn steels considers an expensive and environmentally unfriendly multi-hour batch-like process [ 22 ,  23 ], as it is believed that short soaking times do not allow for full austenite stabilization due to the slow diffusion of manganese [ 24 ,  25 ]. Such process is, however, very time and energy consuming. With prolonging time the initial microstructure tempers [ 26 ] and RA grain size increases [ 27 ], which decreases the mechanical properties of steel. Moreover, due to the sensitivity of the steel to local annealing conditions, there is a risk in case of industrial batch-type annealing of obtaining non-uniform properties depending on a distance from the coil center [ 28 ,  29 ]. Research on IA acceleration has mainly focused on the so-called flash annealing, which involves heating at a rate of ~ 100 °C/s to over 800 °C followed by the immediate quenching. In this case, during the time-efficient process, austenite is stabilized by carbon redistribution, which allows to obtain high-strength properties. However, due to the necessity of using induction heating in the process, it does not have the potential for large-scale application in industry [ 24 ,  25 ].

Our preliminary studies indicated that a significant fraction of RA enriched in Mn may be formed during annealing at 680 °C within only 1 min [ 30 ]. However, the stability of formed RA was too high due to its high enrichment in C and Mn, and a small grain size. Therefore, it could not be utilized fully during next metal forming operations. However, these results indicated the possibility of obtaining steel with a high RA amount and high mechanical properties in case of the further optimizing the fraction and stability of the RA formed in the shortened manufacturing cycle. In response to the research gap and market demand for a sustainable manufacturing process of medium-Mn steels, this study attempts to design from scratch and optimize the process parameters for continuous annealing of medium-Mn steel. This is motivated by the need to design a process that is industrially feasible and can be applied on a large scale. Moreover, it has to be economically viable and can utilize existing machines, tools and infrastructure. To obtain the highest possible mechanical properties, a novel “rapid investigation” methodology was proposed and implemented, using the processing of sub-sized tensile samples in the chamber of the dilatometer with modified tools. It allows for time- and material-efficient experimental verification of numerous heat treatment parameters. In addition to significantly shortening the time from designing processing parameters to verifying the obtained strength properties, it also allows to eliminate the need for mechanical processing of samples after heat treatment. It additionally eliminates the risk of damage/deformation of the surface area of the material. This is important from the viewpoint of possible stress- or strain-induced RA transformation in the metal’s surface layer [ 31 ]. Due to the advantage of hot-rolled steel over cold-rolled steel in terms of mechanical properties, it was decided to test this type of steel especially suitable for underbody elements.

sections.heading: Material production and thermal characterization
paragraphs: Finally, material was hot rolled in a temperature range from 1100 to 750 °C to a thickness of 4.5 mm and air cooled, which resulted in producing a fully martensitic microstructure due to the high hardenability. A high concentration of Mn causes that medium-Mn steels are often not sensitive to cooling conditions due to high hardenability [ 32 ]. The addition of Mo to medium-Mn steels allows for increased both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength without sacrificing total elongation due to the synergistic effects of precipitation hardening and grain refinement. This element increases also the hydrogen embrittlement resistance [ 33 ] and hardenability of the alloy through an M s  decrease [ 34 ,  35 ]. Moreover, Mo increases the C diffusion activation energy in austenite and decreases the C diffusion coefficient. Similarly to Mn, Mo suppresses the formation of grain boundary ferrite, pearlite and acicular ferrite and promotes the formation of bainite [ 36 ,  37 ]. The kinetics of phase transformations during heat treatment was recorded using a Bahr DIL805A/D high-resolution dilatometer on ⌀4 × 10 mm samples. Initial heating and cooling cycles were performed to identify the characteristic temperatures (A c1 , A c3 , M s ), hardenability, and the influence of the heating rate on RA stability. Next intercritical annealing physical simulations were performed for soaking temperatures from 700 to 760 °C and time from 20 to 120 s from which the M s  temperatures were determined. The dilatometer was equipped with fused silica pushrods and a S-type thermocouple. Cooling was performed using helium. Investigations of heating and cooling rates, which are possible to obtain in the electric furnace for different thickness of plates (5, 12 and 20 mm) were performed using a Czylok FCF 5SM-d furnace. Plates with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm and thicknesses of 5/12/20 mm were used. In the core (mid-thickness) of each plate, 20 mm deep holes were drilled into which the K-type thermocouples PCE TF-121/10 and/or Omega HKMQSS-M100U-150 were inserted, and connected to a 4-channel PCE-T390 data logger. The heating rate of steel plates was tested in a furnace with an operating temperature of 800, 900 and 1000 °C. Temperature changes were measured every 1 s during heating in the furnace and cooling of the plates in air with its access on all sides of the plate.

sections.heading: Rapid investigation
paragraphs: For a “rapid investigation” of heat treatment parameters, a novel method of preparing tensile samples was designed. As the high-resolution Bahr DIL805A/D dilatometer allows for an ultra-precise control of temperature–time parameters (due to induction heating, gas cooling and a system controlling temperature by thermocouple welded to the central point of sample), it was used for the heat treatment of specially designed samples. Moreover, protective or vacuum environment may be applied, which prevents decarburization and/or oxidation.

The sample attachment in the device is visible in Fig.  1 a. Shortening the fused-silica push rods or attaching the dilatometer measuring system to distal mounting holes (recommended) allows the attachment of a static tensile test specimen up to 38 mm long. Due to possible differences in the sample temperature with a distance from the induction coil center, a measuring length of 9 mm was used (for a 28 mm wide coil). To enable the sample to be correctly gripped by the testing machine, the grip section is 14 mm. The width of the grip part of the sample must not differ too much from the width of the measuring part of the sample because it behaves like a radiator even under vacuum conditions, which can cause significant temperature changes. The use of the sample geometry shown in Fig.  1 b allows to reduce the temperature difference between the center of the sample, where a thermocouple is attached and the edge of the measuring part to less than 5 °C (Fig.  1 a, c). The designed geometry can be produced by most common methods such as milling, water cutting or electro-discharge cutting. Such mounted samples may be heat treated in the dilatometer under arbitrary temperature–time parameters (Fig.  1 c). Next, it may be directly transferred to a universal testing machine for static tensile tests, which ensures immediate linking between heat treatment parameters and mechanical properties. Fig. 1 Application of rapid investigation in heat treatment:  a  mounting of the proposed sample for a static tensile test in a dilatometer;  b  dimensions of the sub-sized sample for a static tensile test;  c  heat treatment of the sample with newly designed geometry

Moreover, the influence of machining after heat treatment on strength properties of the material is eliminated because the samples after the heat treatment are directly subjected to a tensile test, which is particularly important in case of RA-containing steels, which may eventually transform to martensite during mechanical processing. In addition, thanks to the low thickness-to-width ratio, the proposed sample can be precisely and safely clamped in the jaws of the testing machine by rotating 90° in the tensile axis compared to typical practice (Fig.  2 ). This significantly reduces the risk of the mounting method influencing measurement results. The undersized geometry of the tensile samples may result in obtaining overestimated ductility of tested samples [ 38 ], as the ratio of the cross section to the gauge length is not in accordance with the standard. This causes the ratio of the neck in the tensile sample to its uniformly deformed area to be overstated, which results in obtaining increased values of total elongation [ 39 ]. The use of non-standard samples can, however, be effectively applied for comparative studies as is the case in this work, where samples with the same geometry are tested after treating under different temperature–time conditions. Fig. 2 Fixing of the proposed sample in the testing machine

This methodology was applied to samples annealed at 700–720 °C for 20–120 s, which were selected based on initial dilatometric results. The mechanical testing was performed using the ZWICK 020 tensile machine equipped with an optic extensometer at a nominal strain rate of 10 –3  s −1 .

The specimens were cut from the central part of each sample, ground up to 1200 grit, polished using 1 and 3 μm diamond pasts and finally etched using 3% nital for 3 s at room temperature. The RA fraction and its carbon concentration were determined on the basis of X-ray diffraction measurements [ 40 ] (XRD—X’Pert PRO MPD).

sections.heading: Heating rate
paragraphs: The performed dilatometric tests confirmed that for short soaking (1 min) at 760 °C a significant difference in austenite stability is observed with changing a heating rate as the M s  temperature increases by over 70 °C, when the heating rate increased from 3 to 150 °C/s (Fig.  3 a). Due to the very short holding time, in this case, the heating rate has a significant influence on the period of processing of the steel at temperatures above A c1 —the intercritical range. Also in case of 60 min of soaking a difference of over 30 °C is observed, when the heating rate increases from 3 to 50 °C/s (Fig.  3  b). In this case, the total intercritical processing times for all variants are very similar. These results suggest that the stability of austenite is higher the slower steel is heated to the soaking temperature, regardless of the subsequent soaking time. This phenomenon may be explained by analyzing the mechanism occurring during heating process. According to the literature, during the heating the hot-rolled (martensitic) medium-Mn steel, tempering occurs as first [ 41 ]. Mn-rich cementite precipitates are present inside martensitic laths and on their boundaries [ 42 ]. These areas are subsequently nucleation sites for austenite. In general, when the temperature crosses the A c1  point, the formation and evolution of dual phase microstructure starts. Austenite is formed and starts to grow and simultaneously the redistribution of alloying elements occurs [ 43 ]. Therefore, slow heating rate increases the annealing time as a period between A c1  and a desired annealing temperature is longer. It is especially important in short–continuous annealing lines—where several more seconds in the intercritical region may affect results. Fig. 3 Dilatometric results indicating the influence of the heating rate on M s  temperature for  a  1 min and  b  60 min soaking at 760 °C

The studies by Apple and Krauss [ 41 ] and Han and Lee [ 44 ] have shown that a heating rate influences the cementite precipitation process of the initially martensitic microstructures. The increase in heating rate causes two effects: (1) A c1 , A c3  and the cementite-precipitation-start-temperatures increase. The difference for Fe–9Mn–0.05C (wt.%) steel reached 90 °C, 20 °C and 60 °C, respectively, with the heating rate increase from 0.1 °C/s to 65 °C/s [ 44 ]; (2) when the heating rate increases, the time for nucleation and growth of cementite is reduced, which results in more homogenized redistribution of C and Mn in the microstructure [ 16 ]. It was suggested that it results in less enriched austenite especially in an initial stage of intercritical annealing because some part of C and Mn atoms are still supersaturated in martensite. When a heating rate exceeds ~ 15 °C/s the cementite-precipitation-start-temperature may not be recorded by dilatometry anymore. It indicates the transition of reversed transformation mechanism from diffusive to diffusionless. Such effect was first observed in stainless steels [ 45 ]. In typical diffusive reversed transformation, the formed austenite is already enriched in C and Mn as it nucleates in areas rich in the mentioned elements. In diffusionless reversed transformation, the formed austenite has the same chemical composition as the initial martensite. It was noticed that it prolongs significantly the time needed for austenite stabilization and decreases its overall stability compared to slower-heated steels [ 44 ].

This type of slow heating is realized in the case of batch annealing, which is, however, a long-term process. To enable sustainable industrial production of medium manganese steels, it would be advantageous to use continuous annealing, which provides relatively fast heating and short soaking times [ 46 ]. The heating curves (Fig.  4 a-c) and instantaneous heating rates (Fig.  4 d-f) that may be obtained in common electric furnaces for different thicknesses of steel plates are shown in Fig.  4 . The heating of steel plates increases with reducing its thickness and increasing the furnace temperature (Fig.  4 a–c). For 5 mm plate the time needed to achieve 750 °C decreases from ~ 317 to ~ 107 s with increasing the furnace temperature from 800 to 1000 °C (Fig.  4 a). In case of 20 mm plate, it is ~ 1083 s and 394 s, respectively (Fig.  4 c). The heating rate decreases continuously during the heating of plates (Fig.  4 d–f). At the furnace temperature of 1000 °C the heating rate decreases from 14 °C/s, 5 °C/s, and 3.2 °C/s at room temperature to 4.7 °C/s, 1.8 °C/s, and 1.3 °C/s at 600 °C for plates with thicknesses of 5, 12 and 20 mm, respectively. As the heating rate changes significantly during heating to the soaking temperature it is necessary to define boundary conditions. Fig. 4 Time–temperature changes and real heating rate of plates with different thicknesses  a ,  d  5 mm,  b ,  e  12 mm,  c ,  f  20 mm dependent on set electric furnace temperature

For this purpose, dilatometric tests were carried out to identify a temperature at which martensite tempering begins, i.e., the precipitation of carbides (P s )—and a temperature at which the austenitic transformation begins (A c1 ) (Fig.  5 ). They are 439 and 633 °C, respectively. Thus, these are the temperatures at which the heating rate plays a special role as indicated in [ 44 ]. Figure  6  summarizes the influence of plate thickness and furnace temperature on the heating rate in the range of (a) 400–720 °C and (b) 600–720 °C. In case of the temperature range 400–720 °C the heating rate for the furnace temperature of 1000 °C decreases from about 11 to 2 °C/s with the plate thickness change from 5 to 20 mm. In case of the furnace temperature of 800 °C, it is 2 and 0.7 °C/s, respectively. In case of the heating range from 600 to 720 °C the heating rate in the furnace at 800 °C is below 1 °C/s and at 1000 °C it is below 3.5 °C/s for all analyzed plate thicknesses. Taking into account both tests on the influence of heating rate on austenite stability (Fig.  3 ) and possible heating rates in the electric furnace (Fig.  6 ), for dilatometric simulations of intercritical annealing an average heating rate of 3 °C/s was selected, which is intended to prevent diffusionless transformation and is possible to apply under industrial conditions [ 47 ,  48 ]. Fig. 5 A dilatometric diagram of phase transformation during slow heating of investigated steel Fig. 6 Average heating rates of plates with different thicknesses in the range from  a  400 to 720 °C, and  b  600 to 720 °C dependent on a set furnace temperature

sections.heading: Cooling rate
paragraphs: The accelerated cooling methods like water spray or water mist [ 49 ] are frequently used in case of industrial production processes for steel sheets. However, in the case of producing a product with a larger cross section and thus heat capacity like plates and forgings, which requires longer cooling times, it is important that heat treatment results in maintaining a uniform microstructure over the entire cross section. To enable the most flexible production process with a wide technological window, good if the material is not sensitive to the cooling rate and may be cooled both fast and slow even using air. For this purpose, tests were carried out to investigate the possibility of cooling the analyzed alloy using air without changing the microstructure.

First, experiments were carried out to determine a cooling rate of plates of different thicknesses in air (Fig.  7 ). As expected, the cooling time from ~ 700 °C to 150 °C increases from ~ 793 s to ~ 2116 s with an increase of plate thickness from 5 to 20 mm (Fig.  7 a). The cooling rate for such plates reaches initially 1 °C/s and 3 °C/s, respectively, and next decreases with a decrease of the plate’s temperature below 200 °C to less than 0.3 °C/s. As the temperature in plates’ core and surface may vary due to differences in heat reception, an additional experiment was carried out using a 20 mm-thick plate (Fig.  8 ), where the cooling rates were tested at different plate depths (10, 5 and 2 mm) (Fig.  8 a). Interestingly, the results showed that the steel was cooled at a remarkably similar rate over the entire cross section (Fig.  8 b), with a temperature difference of max. 10 °C between the core and the surface-close area (Fig.  8 c). Fig. 7 Time–temperature changes and real cooling rate of plates with different thicknesses in air cooling Fig. 8 Mounting of thermocouples and the geometry of the steel plate ( a ), time–temperature changes during air cooling ( b ), and changes of temperature records between different points of measurement ( c )

To validate the possibility of implementation air cooling in terms of phase transformations during cooling, dilatometric tests with applied different cooling rates were conducted (Fig.  9 ). They indicated that cooling at different rates from 60 to 0.1 °C/s (which is lower than the air cooling rate) after austenitization of steel at 1000 °C results only in martensitic transformation. The recorded M s  temperature was very similar for all applied cooling rates (~ 317 °C). This experiment confirmed that due to increased concentration of Mn and Mo in steel its hardenability is significantly increased, which prevents any other phase transitions during cooling apart from the martensitic transformation. As the high-temperature-dual-phase microstructure may affect the kinetics of phase transformation during cooling, also tests including different cooling rates were performed after intercritical annealing at 680 °C for 60 min. Such temperature and soaking time of investigated steel ensures the high-temperature microstructure of over 30% austenite in a ferritic matrix [ 30 ]. These investigations also indicated the lack of sensitivity of the steel to a cooling rate, as during cooling no transformation occurred. These studies finally confirmed the possibility of using both accelerated and air cooling of the alloy after intercritical annealing, which increases the process flexibility. Taking into account both tests on air cooling rate (Fig.  7 ) and its influence on phase transformations during cooling (Fig.  9 ), an average cooling rate of 1 °C/s was selected as proper for implementation of dilatometric simulations of intercritical annealing. Fig. 9 Dilatometric results of the influence of cooling rate on phase transformations of samples after  a  austenitization at 1000 °C and  b  intercritical annealing at 680 °C for 60 min

sections.heading: Rapid investigation of intercritical annealing
paragraphs: Lee and de Cooman [ 50 ] suggested that for medium-Mn steels, optimal intercritical annealing should be performed at a temperature slightly lower than the one at which martensite forms during the cooling process. These rules are also confirmed in other works [ 16 ,  51 ]. To define the area of interest, dilatometric tests were performed to determine the time and temperature limits after exceeding which the martensitic transformation of austenite occurs in the steel. Our previous studies have shown that at a temperature of 680 °C and annealing for 1 min [ 30 ], a full stabilization of the formed austenite is possible. For this reason, the temperature range of 700–760 °C was selected for the new tests. Due to the continuous nature of performed annealing the time between 20 and 120 s was selected for the trials. Changes in M s  temperature (austenite stability) depending on an applied temperature and soaking time are present in Tables  1 ,  2 . They indicate that austenite produced in steel during soaking is fully stable below the soaking temperature of 730 °C. Only at 720 °C and soaking time of 120 s the M s  temperature of 45 °C was identified by dilatometry. Therefore, this temperature–time range (marked by the red frame in Table  2 ) was selected for the further test involving a newly proposed method of “rapid investigation” in heat treatment. The newly designed tensile samples were heat treated in the dilatometer in a temperature range from 700 to 720 °C and within the time range from 20 to 120 s. Next, they were directly subjected to sub-sized static tensile tests, which significantly shortened the time required to link mechanical results and heat treatment parameters. Results of strength and plasticity from this test are summarized and color marked in Table  3 . In general, the yield strength (YS) decreases with an increase of soaking temperature and time (from 795 MPa after soaking at 700 °C for 20 s to 518 MPa for soaking at 720 °C for 120 s), while ultimate tensile strength (UTS) increases (from 937 MPa after soaking at 700 °C for 20 s to 1228 MPa for soaking at 720 °C for 120 s). It gives an increase of strain hardening (SH—which is the stress increase between YS and UTS) from 142 MPa after soaking at 700 °C for 20 s to over 700 MPa for soaking at 720 °C within 120 s. In case of total elongation and the UTS x TEl product, there is not so clear tendency. The highest elongation of over 36% was obtained for soaking at 700 °C for 40 s and 710 °C for 20 s. In case of UTS x TEl product the highest values of over 36 GPa% were obtained for soaking at 710 °C for 20 and 40 s (Fig.  10 ). For annealing at 710 and 720 °C for 60 s a decrease in the UTS x TEl product is visible while in case of annealing at 700 °C a peak of the UTS x TEl product after such annealing time was recorded. Despite relatively minor differences in the applied temperature–time parameters of heat treatment, very large differences in mechanical properties were obtained. On the one hand, this is beneficial because it allows obtaining a wide range of mechanical properties without significant interference in the parameters of the production process. On the other hand, however, it means a rather narrow technological window for both time and temperature of the annealing. This is the effect of implementing the ART process under strongly non-equilibrium conditions. Studies on medium-Mn steels clearly indicate that the formation of austenite is very rapid in the first 30–60 min of the process [ 22 ,  52 ], after which its fraction begins to stabilize [ 23 ]. Obtaining the equilibrium fraction may take up to several hours [ 30 ]. The necessity of using non-equilibrium conditions results from the nature of the continuous annealing process, in which time plays a key role. In the case of batch annealing, the heating stage lasts even several dozen hours. It results in conditions close to equilibrium, so even significant differences in time do not affect mechanical properties so significantly. However, even in this case, small changes in temperature have an effect on the RA amount and stability, which was proven in the work [ 53 ], where steel was annealed for a week at different temperatures. Therefore, regardless of the processing mode, it can be stated that medium manganese steels are sensitive to the temperature and time of intercritical annealing, which must be taken into account when planning production.

The matrix of mechanical properties (Table  3 ) prepared in the time-efficient way by proposed “rapid investigation” presented in this paper allows for the selection of appropriate heat treatment parameters for a given steel application. For example, if the achievement of the highest possible plasticity and a UTS x TEl product is the target—a process utilizing 2-zone furnace indicated in Fig.  11  could be implemented. The furnace heating zone temperature is dependent on a plate thickness, to allow reaching a heating rate above a temperature at which carbides start to precipitate (~ 400 °C), in the range from ~ 2 to 5 °C/s. The soaking time in the annealing zone of furnace at 710 °C should last from 20 to 40 s and the final cooling may be performed in air. Such a process should allow obtaining advanced high-strength and ductile steel with YS of ~ 660 MPa, UTS of ~ 1020 MPa, and TEl of ~ 35%. Fig. 11 The proposed sustainable and cost-effective heat treatment schedule, which can be implemented under industrial conditions

sections.heading: Microstructure–strength relationships
paragraphs: For a better understanding the differences in mechanical properties a microstructural analysis was performed (Fig.  12 ). The microstructures were next compared to the mechanical behavior (Fig.  12 c,f,i) of specific samples. The microstructure of the sample exhibiting the lowest elongation and tensile strength (Fig.  12  a,b) is composed of ferritic matrix and a number of precipitates. Moreover, fine laths of RA are present at the boundaries of the former martensite. According to XRD measurements the RA fraction is about 14% with the carbon concentration of 0.79 wt.%. The microstructures taken at the magnification of 2500 × for samples exhibiting the highest elongation (Fig.  12 d) and the highest strength (Fig.  12 g) at first glance look alike. Both of them have the ultrafine grain size and elongated morphology. The microstructures are composed of bright laths, which may be classified as RA and finer and larger ferrite grains (dark background). According to XRD measurements the RA fraction in the sample exhibiting the highest elongation is 32% with the carbon concentration of 0.46 wt.%, whereas in the one with the highest strength is 21% with the carbon concentration of 0.31 wt.%. To explain the differences in mechanical properties, it is necessary to analyze some details of the microstructure using a higher magnification of 20,000x. This approach reveals that the microstructure of the highest plasticity sample (soaked for 20 s at 710 °C) has homogeneously looking RA grains (Fig.  12 e), whereas in the microstructure of highest strength sample (soaked for 120 s at 720 °C) some of the RA grains have a non-homogeneous, "rough" morphology (Fig.  12 h). This clearly indicates the presence of fresh martensite in the structure, which is a product of the transformation occurring during the final cooling (recorded also by dilatometry). This explains why, despite the longest process and its highest temperature, the measurement of the RA fraction showed a lower value than for the sample soaked for 20 s at 710 °C. Since this martensite is formed by the transformation of austenite, it is located in the primary austenitic laths. The "roughness" of this phase in microscopic images is a characteristic feature resulting from its susceptibility to nital etching [ 54 ]. The 700 °C–20 s sample (Fig.  12 c) shows the highest YS among analyzed samples; however, its strain hardening is very low. Therefore, necking occurs at a low strain level. What is remarkable here, the post necking elongation is over 3 times higher than uniform elongation. In case of 710 °C–20 s sample YS is lower by over 120 MPa; however, it is recompensated by much more intense strain hardening, which postpones necking from the elongation of below 10% to over 25%. The post necking elongation is significantly reduced in this sample. For the highest-strength sample (Fig.  12 i) the YS decreases even further, which is compensated by the most intense strain hardening among all the samples. It allows to increase the stress from YS to UTS by 710 MPa. However, due to high strength, the elongation in these samples is reduced. Fig. 12 Comparison of the microstructure–strength relationships for samples with the lowest ductility and lowest strength ( a – c ), most ductile ( d – f ) and with the highest strength ( g - i ) obtained during performed rapid investigation; F—ferrite, RA—retained austenite, M—martensite, θ—carbides

A better understanding of the plastic deformation behavior is provided by the instantaneous strain hardening exponent ( n ) changes present in Fig.  13 b. Previous studies on this steel [ 30 ,  55 ,  56 ] indicated that a rapid increase of  n  value is related to the intense SIMT, while its peak and next drop are related to the exhaustion of TRIP effect. In case of the 700 °C–20 s sample despite initial 14% of RA no relevant strain hardening was observed. The  n  value reached only about 0.11. Such behavior is exhibited in steel where despite the presence of RA the SIMT and TRIP effect do not occur due to too high stability [ 30 ]. In such microstructure mainly the ferritic matrix contributes to the mechanical properties. In 710 °C–20 s sample a moderate and continuous increase in  n  value occurs up to 0.21 strain, which in general is favorable in case of mechanical properties as it indicates a constant and gradual transformation of RA into martensite, which improves simultaneously strength and plasticity. In case of the 720 °C—120 s sample the  n  value has much higher values throughout the entire range of uniform deformation (reaching up to 0.4, which is 25% more than in case of the SIA sample). In this sample, as suggested by changes in  n  values, a rapid SIMT effect occurs at low strain levels. It leads to a fast exhaustion of the TRIP effect and dynamic increase of the strain-induced martensite in the microstructure. This decelerates the further strain hardening and increase in plasticity. This is indicated by a maximum in the value of  n  and an inflection point of the function, after which the strain hardening starts to decrease rapidly. Such maximum point is also present in case of 720 °C—120 s sample. However, the initial increase in  n  value is gradual and the peak is much less sharp and the subsequent decline is gradual. It suggests much more gradual and homogeneous SIMT within the entire deformation range. The serrations observed in case of 720 °C—120 s sample (Fig.  12 i) may confirm the low RA stability in this sample. Such relation was pointed in other works [ 30 ,  56 ]. sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The work addressed the design and optimization of continuous annealing of advanced 0.16C-4.7Mn-1.6Al-0.2Si-0.2Mo medium-Mn steel by utilizing “rapid investigation” of heat treatment. The “rapid investigation” in heat treatment method utilizing the high-precision temperature–time control was proposed in this paper. Results proved that the investigated medium-Mn steel may be fully produced under conditions of continuous annealing process utilizing installations available in the industry. The research led to the following conclusions: The new method of “rapid investigation” in heat treatment performed by the high-precision temperature–time control in the dilatometer with modified tools allowed for producing deformation-free sub-size tensile samples with a total length of 38 mm. They were next used for time-efficient optimization and verification of the process parameters for targeted mechanical properties. A heating rate had a determining effect on the M s  temperature and thus the stability of austenite. An increase in a heating rate from 3 to 150 °C/s led to a significant increase in M s  temperature (over 30 °C) even after 1 h of soaking. Air cooling and furnace heating rates possible to obtain in an electric furnace were characterized for different plate thicknesses. It was possible to obtain a favorable heating rate of 2–5 °C in the temperature range of 400–720 °C allowing for diffusive austenitic transformation and utilization in the continuous line using electric furnace heated up to a range from 800 to 1000 °C, depending on a plate thickness. The analyzed 4.7 wt.% Mn steel was insensitive to a cooling rate due to high hardenability, which allowed for its air cooling corresponding to an average cooling rate below 1 °C/s. Continuous annealing of hot-rolled medium-Mn steels resulted in the formation of a lath morphology with a ferritic matrix decorated with retained austenite at the boundaries, the thickness of which increased significantly and the stability decreased with the extension of the soaking time even below 120 s. The applied cost and time-efficient heat treatment processes allowed to obtain the advanced multiphase steel with the UTSxTEl product in the range between 27 and 37 GPa%, which may provide a wide range of mechanical applications requiring high plasticity and/or high strength.
